# The Deployment Lifecycle {#sec-deployment-lifecycle}

Deployment is a controlled state transition from a known baseline to a
candidate. The terms of that transition form the deployment release contract:
the compatibility conditions the candidate must meet, the evidence required to
widen exposure, and the recovery action for each failure. A successful build
shows that the artifacts exist. The contract supplies the three further
assurances a release needs: the candidate can coexist with the live system, the
comparison against the baseline is trustworthy, and service can be recovered.

This chapter takes the integration release from @sec-wiring-stack, the versioned
statement of what the stack connects and what evidence makes it safe to
release, and turns it into an operated change. The unit of control is a
release manifest: a signed record that composes the revisions used by a
behavior, even when those parts are separately deployed. The lifecycle ends
only when desired and observed state agree, the evidence is attached, and a
release owner accepts the remaining risk. The output is a deployment release
record.

Production ML exposed this problem before generative AI. Learning code is a
small part of a deployed ML system; data dependencies, configuration, serving,
and monitoring create most of its operational surface [@sculley2015debt]. The
ML Test Score consequently treats data, model, infrastructure, and monitoring
tests as production-readiness evidence [@breck2017mltestscore]. Generative AI
adds prompts, retrieval, tools, policies, stochastic evaluation, and often a
hosted model whose implementation the operator cannot inspect. It enlarges the
release state, and the earlier engineering obligations still apply.

## Name the release state

A model checkpoint, the saved file of trained weights, is one artifact among
the several that a release combines. A release manifest binds the
behavior-bearing components to one reviewable identity. A deployment event maps
that manifest to an environment and cohort. Observed runtime state then records
what is actually serving. The three records stay separate because an approved
manifest does not show that every cell has converged to it.

The manifest should fingerprint at least the following surfaces.

| Surface | Identity to record |
|---|---|
| Inference | model revision, tokenizer or chat template, adapter, serving runtime, decoding policy |
| Context | prompt revision, retrieval snapshot, corpus and index revision, embedding and reranking pipeline |
| Action | tool implementation and tool schema, permission and policy revision, effect class |
| Routing | router configuration, fallback order, feature flags, assignment policy |
| State | API and event schema, data schema, serializer, cache namespace, migration phase |
| Operation | infrastructure digest, region or cell, telemetry schema, evaluator revision |
| Mutable dependency | endpoint, provider revision, region, declared mutability, evidence expiry, probe, fallback, kill switch |

Controllable artifacts use immutable content digests rather than mutable tags
such as `latest`. Secret values never belong in the manifest; it records only a
scoped secret-version reference. A hosted API, live tool, or changing corpus may
not offer byte identity. In that case the manifest records the limitation as a
bounded mutable dependency with an owner, evidence expiry, change-detection
probe, requalification rule, and fallback. An opaque provider identifier is
evidence of which revision served, and it falls short of byte reproducibility.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-deploy-bundle
//| fig-cap: "A release manifest composes immutable artifacts and bounded mutable dependencies. The deployment event assigns it to an environment; observed state proves what actually serves."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.18; ranksep=0.24;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1, width=2.25];
  edge [fontsize=8, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  A [label="Artifacts\ncode · model · prompt\nretrieval · tools · policy"];
  M [label="Signed release manifest\ndigests · schemas · evidence\nowner · expiry · recovery"];
  D [label="Deployment event\nenvironment · cell · cohort"];
  O [label="Observed state\nactual revisions · health"];
  A -> M [label="compose"];
  M -> D [label="authorize"];
  D -> O [label="reconcile"];
}
```

Each supply-chain control establishes one narrow property. A digest proves byte
identity. A signature authenticates a statement, such as who published the
bytes, under a trust policy. A software bill of materials inventories the
declared composition. Provenance records how a build was produced. None of them
shows that the release is safe, correct, or built from benign source, so
admission checks them together: the artifact digest, signed manifest,
attestation subject, allowed builder and source, and software bill of
materials. Supply-chain provenance such as SLSA and in-toto makes that chain
inspectable [@slsa2025spec; @torresarias2019intoto]. Update metadata should
also resist a rollback attack, freeze attack, or mix-and-match of revisions that
were never approved together, the threats formalized by The Update Framework
[@tuf2026spec].

The manifest records the system fingerprint, but the release record also needs
scope, owner, authority, acceptance evidence, known gaps, expiry, desired state,
observed state, and recovery target. Every request, conversation, or long-running
job records its assigned release so an incident can be traced to the behavior
that handled it.

## Separate the lifecycle verbs

Each lifecycle verb names a distinct transition.

- **Deploy** makes a candidate available in an environment without necessarily
  exposing users.
- **Release** activates the candidate for a declared cohort.
- **Promote** widens exposure after the required evidence passes.
- **Abort** stops a transition before more exposure or irreversible work occurs.
- **Rollback** restores a previous compatible serving path.
- **Roll forward** deploys a repair when reversal is unsafe or impossible.

A feature flag can separate deployment from release. A rolling update replaces
capacity while old and new versions coexist. Blue-green maintains two
environments and switches traffic; it becomes a canary only if both receive
concurrent traffic. A canary is a partial, time-limited release evaluated
against a control [@warner2018canarying]. The mechanism follows from the state
and risk being changed; none is universally safest.

## Prove coexistence before exposure

During a rollout, old and new code run at the same time. The compatibility
envelope, meaning every interface and piece of state that old and new versions
must both handle correctly, therefore extends beyond request and response
types. It includes the API and event schema, data schema and serializer, old
reader and new reader, old writer and new writer, retrieval index generations,
cache namespaces, session state, checkpoint state, queued jobs, and tool-effect
records. The old version must safely interpret what the candidate can write if
traffic rollback is meant to remain available.

The fixtures below test both directions before production.

| Fixture | Question answered |
|---|---|
| Old client to new server; new client to old server | Are request and response contracts compatible? |
| Old reader after new writer; new reader after old writer | Can mixed versions share persisted state? |
| Half-old and half-new fleet | Do routing, cache, queue, and session semantics survive coexistence? |
| Upgrade, candidate write, then downgrade | Does the promised rollback actually preserve data? |
| Long session and queued job across cutover | Is release identity sticky for stateful work? |
| Migration retry and restore | Are migration steps idempotent, observable, and recoverable? |

AWS's rollback-safety guidance describes the same ordering for distributed
deployments: readers learn a new form before any writer produces it, and on the
way back the order reverses [@pokkunuri2019rollback]. The conformance test
matrix should run in CI and in a production-like environment with the real
serializers, queues, schemas, and adapters. A passing unit test against one
version cannot prove mixed-version compatibility.

When a schema cannot change in one compatible step, the change follows
**expand, migrate, contract** [@sato2014parallel]. The expand step extends
readers and schemas to accept both forms while writers keep producing the old
form. The migrate step dual-reads or dual-writes where necessary, backfills with
resumable checkpoints, and verifies counts, referential integrity, and semantic
equivalence. The new form is activated only after mixed versions pass. The
contract step comes in a later release, after old readers, old writers,
sessions, and jobs are gone and the rollback window has closed. Once the old
form is removed, a release that depends on it can no longer be restored, so the
removal is declared as a recovery boundary.

## Promote by widening evidence and exposure

Promotion begins with build and verification, before any user traffic. The
first stage verifies digests, signatures, provenance, configuration, schemas,
capacity, credentials, and the compatibility fixtures. The offline gate from
@sec-eval-practice then runs deterministic invariants and quality estimates
over representative slices, named subsets of cases that are judged separately.
A dark launch starts the candidate and its dependencies without routing
requests, revealing startup, capacity, and control-plane faults.

Shadow execution sends a copy of live requests to the candidate and discards
its responses. It can expose gaps between an offline set and live inputs, and
it carries its own risks. Duplicating a request may disclose data, consume
provider quota, pollute a shared cache, mutate shared state, or execute a tool.
A safe shadow path must apply current authorization before duplication, suppress
side effects, use sandboxed tools, restrict egress, use an isolated cache and
isolated state, cap load, quarantine its traces, and discard the candidate
output. Some workloads cannot be shadowed safely.

User-facing exposure starts with a limited cell, then a sticky canary, one that
keeps each assigned unit on the same release for the length of the test. The
rollout plan declares that assignment unit: tenant, user, session, conversation,
or task. When state or experience can carry over, the chosen unit is one that
keeps each workflow on a single side, candidate or baseline. The canary runs
against a concurrent control, and the rollout records both the planned
assignment and the actual exposure. Telemetry is labeled by observed release.
Outcomes are interpreted only after a test for sample ratio mismatch, a gap
between the planned and the observed allocation, which can reveal assignment or
instrumentation faults [@fabijan2019srm].

```{dot}
//| label: fig-deploy-pipeline
//| fig-cap: "Promotion widens evidence before blast radius. Every stage can advance, hold, contain, roll back, or roll forward; missing evidence never advances the release."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.13; ranksep=0.20;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1, width=2.25];
  edge [fontsize=8, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  B [label="Build and verify\nsupply chain · compatibility"];
  O [label="Offline gate\ninvariants · evals · slices"];
  D [label="Dark launch + shadow\ncapacity · isolated replay"];
  C [label="Cell + sticky canary\nconcurrent control"];
  R [label="Regional waves\nbake · widen parallelism"];
  F [label="Full release\nreconcile · observe"];
  B -> O -> D -> C -> R -> F;
}
```

Regional waves bound correlated failure. The first wave is a small but
representative cell, and the next is a contrasting or higher-volume region.
Parallelism increases only after a bake period. Each wave preserves failover
capacity and capacity headroom, honors residency and local dependency
constraints, and never updates every replica in one failure domain together.
Where possible, each comparison carries one active change so that its effect
remains attributable. Routing and configuration are published atomically from a
last-known-good record, and every wave shares the same global stop condition.
This staged shape follows established hands-off deployment practice
[@liguori2020deployments].

## Make the gate answer the release question

Deterministic checks and statistical checks answer different questions. Schema
validation, authorization, policy, idempotency, tool permission, migration
integrity, and route identity are deterministic invariants: one violation blocks
promotion. Statistical comparison runs alongside them and estimates uncertain
quality or performance differences over a population.

The quality condition asks whether, with stated confidence, the candidate
is worse than the control by no more than a tolerated amount. For required
metric or slice $j$, define

$$
\Delta_j = \mathbb{E}[Y_j(1)-Y_j(0)],
$$

where $Y_j(1)$ is the candidate outcome and $Y_j(0)$ the concurrent-control
outcome for the same declared population. Let $L_j$ be a valid lower confidence
bound for $\Delta_j$, and let $\delta_j \geq 0$ be the predeclared practical
loss, or non-inferiority margin, the service can tolerate. A necessary quality
condition is

$$
L_j \geq -\delta_j
\qquad \text{for all required } j.
$$

The quality condition is one part of the gate. Before the release, the plan
declares one primary metric, guardrail metrics, minimum detectable effects,
slices, minimum traffic, dwell time, and delayed outcome window. The gate
requires complete evidence and fails closed when assignment, exposure,
evaluator, or telemetry data is missing. An absolute SLO and harm boundary
applies even when the candidate looks better than a failing control. Shared
failure, interference between cohorts, carryover from earlier assignments,
novelty effects, and a delayed outcome can all invalidate a naive comparison.
Online controlled-experiment practice provides the experimental foundation for
these checks [@kohavi2009experiments].

A fixed-horizon interval is computed once, at a sample size chosen in advance;
checking it repeatedly until it passes changes its error rate. A gate therefore
uses either a fixed horizon or an always-valid method designed for continuous
monitoring and optional stopping [@johari2022alwaysvalid]. A result of “no
significant difference” is not evidence of safety, because the experiment may be
underpowered. Promotion requires the predeclared bounds and operational
guardrails to pass; an absence of alerts does not satisfy that requirement.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

Stochastic generation means exact output bytes are usually the wrong quality
contract (@sec-serving-problem). The serving layer pushes quality
comparison toward population estimates, while schema, permission, side-effect,
and state contracts remain exact checks. The release gate therefore joins the
evaluation evidence of @sec-eval-practice with the boundary contracts of
@sec-wiring-stack and the authorization rules of @sec-security-authorization.
:::

## Detect changes after promotion

A release's behavior can change without a new model. Configuration drift,
policy drift, retrieval-corpus or index drift, schema drift, tool drift,
evaluator drift, telemetry drift, runtime drift, and infrastructure drift can all
change observed behavior. Self-hosted systems drift as well, because mutable
tags, kernels, hardware, caches, and live data can change under them.

For a hosted dependency, the manifest pins an immutable revision where the
provider offers one and records the response model or provider revision actually
observed. When the provider exposes only a mutable alias, the operator shortens
the evidence expiry, runs a change-detection probe, tracks deprecation notices,
and requires requalification before or immediately after an identity change.
The provider's retirement notice period, and whether requests to a retired model
fail or are redirected, are contract terms reviewed when the model is chosen
(@sec-choosing-model). Fixed probes make an otherwise silent change visible,
though they cannot establish complete equivalence. Production failures should
feed a curated regression set through the data loop in @sec-data-engine; raw
trace replay still requires current authorization and side-effect isolation.

Desired and observed state are reconciled continuously in every cell, because
the control plane can report healthy while a replica serves the wrong prompt,
index, or policy. Mixed-version detection, release-labeled telemetry, and
periodic black-box probes close that gap.

## Match recovery to the changed state

Recovery has several actions. An abort stops further exposure. A traffic
rollback routes new work to a compatible earlier release. A state restore
recovers persisted data to a known point. Feature disable or a kill switch
contains one capability. Credential revoke limits a compromised dependency.
Compensate reconciles an external effect that cannot be erased. Roll forward
repairs a state the previous release cannot safely read. Each action addresses
a different kind of change, so one cannot stand in for another.

Rollback counts as safe only after these conditions have been shown: the
previous artifact is retained and loadable, its credentials and dependencies
remain valid, sufficient capacity headroom exists, its readers are
backward-compatible with current persisted and queued state, and no
irreversible effect crosses the declared recovery window. The release record
states the recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO)
[@nist2010contingency]. Unlike a routing change, backup restoration is a
recovery procedure with measurable data loss and duration.

Each change is classified before rollout into one of three recovery classes.

- **Reversible:** traffic rollback to the previous release restores service.
- **Recoverable:** state restore or an explicit compensate action is also
  required.
- **Roll-forward-only:** rollback becomes unsafe after a named migration or
  external effect.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-recovery-path
//| fig-cap: "Recovery follows the state that changed. Abort stops a ramp; Restore adds state recovery or compensation; Roll forward repairs a state that an older release cannot safely consume."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.14; ranksep=0.22;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1, width=1.35];
  edge [fontsize=8, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  X [label="Release fails a gate"];
  A [label="Abort\nhold exposure"];
  Q [label="Old release reads\ncurrent state safely?"];
  T [label="Traffic rollback"];
  S [label="State/effect changed?"];
  R [label="Restore\nor compensate"];
  F [label="Roll forward\nrepair current state"];
  V [label="Recovery verification"];
  X -> A -> Q;
  Q -> T [label="yes"];
  Q -> F [label="no"];
  T -> S;
  S -> V [label="no"];
  S -> R [label="yes"];
  R -> V;
  F -> V;
}
```

Recovery continues after traffic stops. The recovery plan states whether to
drain or cancel in-flight requests, how to handle a queue and backlog, which
long sessions retain their assignment, and how to prevent mixed-version writers
during recovery. The tool-effect records and external side effects are then
reconciled. Recovery verification follows: it compares desired and observed
manifest hashes per cell, runs black-box tasks and deterministic invariants,
inspects SLO and policy metrics, validates data and serializer integrity,
inspects queues and caches, checks dependencies, and verifies the telemetry path
itself. RTO and RPO are measured, the system is observed through a bake period,
and recovery closes only when explicit termination criteria pass. NIST recovery
guidance likewise requires plans, testing, restoration validation, and
continued monitoring [@nist2016recovery].

When impact or uncertainty is material, an incident is declared early. The
response assigns an incident commander, operations lead, communications lead,
release owner, and recorder, freezes unrelated releases, and maintains a
timeline of evidence, decisions, and observed impact. Mitigation restores safe
service. Root-cause analysis can continue after the emergency. Clear roles and a
working record keep those jobs from competing during response
[@mace2018incident].

## Drill the failure paths

The release procedure is software and needs its own conformance test and failure
matrix.

| Failure | Required response and proof |
|---|---|
| Underpowered or misassigned canary | Hold; verify assignment, actual exposure, sample ratio, power, and dwell |
| Shadow side effect or data-policy breach | Stop shadowing; contain effects; audit duplicated data and authorization |
| Missing or stale telemetry | Fail closed; prove the telemetry path before resuming |
| Partial regional rollout | Stop new waves; reconcile desired and observed state cell by cell |
| Schema incompatibility after candidate writes | Block traffic rollback; restore or roll forward according to the migration record |
| Failed rollback or restore | Escalate the incident; isolate writers; preserve evidence; use the tested alternate recovery path |
| Provider alias change or deprecation | Mark existing evidence stale; identify the observed revision; requalify or activate the fallback |
| Recovery appears healthy but user tasks fail | Keep the incident open; repeat black-box and data-integrity verification |

The drills cover mixed-fleet upgrade and downgrade, rollback after candidate
writes, backup restore, regional evacuation, control-plane failure, telemetry
failure, and effect compensation. A recovery plan counts as recovery evidence
only after it has restored a representative state.

## The complete lifecycle

For each candidate:

1. Freeze the signed release manifest, trust evidence, owner, scope, expiry,
   compatibility envelope, rollout policy, and recovery class.
2. Build and verify artifact identity, provenance, schemas, configuration,
   capacity, credentials, and mixed-version conformance fixtures.
3. Pass the offline gate: deterministic invariants, representative quality
   estimates, safety policy, migration checks, and recovery prerequisites.
4. Dark launch, then shadow only where data handling and effect isolation have
   been proved.
5. Release to a limited cell and sticky canary with a concurrent control,
   recorded assignment and exposure, minimum dwell, and complete telemetry.
6. Promote through regional waves only while deterministic blockers, absolute
   guardrails, and predeclared non-inferiority bounds pass.
7. Complete the migration only after the rollback window closes; reconcile
   desired and observed state and retain the last-known-good recovery path.
8. Record evidence, incidents, deviations, RTO/RPO results, known gaps, expiry,
   and the owner who accepted the final state.

The output is a deployment release record. It says what was intended, what
actually ran, why exposure widened, what changed during the transition, and
which recovery path was proved. The next chapter asks how to define reliability
for the nondeterministic behavior now serving users (@sec-reliability).

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

- **How representative the first canary should be.** A low-risk internal cohort
  limits harm but can miss production load and behavior. A representative
  cohort improves inference but accepts more exposure. The manifest should state
  which objective the first wave serves.
- **Fixed horizon or continuous decision.** A fixed horizon is simpler to audit;
  an always-valid design can stop earlier while preserving its error guarantee.
  Switching after looking at the data invalidates either plan.
- **How long to preserve downgrade compatibility.** A longer rollback window
  improves recoverability but delays schema contraction and raises operating
  cost. The deployment release contract records this decision instead of leaving
  it to an ad hoc cleanup.
:::
